claims.text: A high density of nanocrystalline grain boundaries in high-entropy-alloy transition-metal catalysts increases the number of catalytic sites.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries increase catalytic-site activity by locally modifying electronic structure.
The grain-boundary-induced electronic modification lowers activation barriers for reactant adsorption and reaction.
Lower adsorption and reaction barriers enhance catalytic rate.
A high density of nanocrystalline grain boundaries enhances catalyst durability.
Conventionally fabricated comparison catalysts have coarse grains with average grain size greater than 500 nm and low grain-boundary density.
Selective laser melting is a viable method for fabricating high-entropy alloys.
Rapid solidification by selective laser melting or spark plasma sintering will produce an average grain size below 100 nm and increase grain-boundary density.
The comparison should hold alloy composition constant while varying microstructure.
The proposed catalytic comparison is conducted at 300–600 K under otherwise identical reactive conditions.
Grain boundaries provide high-energy defect sites with altered electronic properties that facilitate reactant adsorption and activation.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries mitigate surface poisoning.
Nanocrystalline catalysts will exhibit at least a 20% increase in reaction rate or turnover frequency relative to coarse-grained catalysts.
Nanocrystalline catalysts will show improved long-term stability relative to coarse-grained catalysts.
The mechanism is expected to apply to high-configurational-entropy transition-metal catalysts, including refractory HEAs, when surface adsorption and diffusion are rate-limiting.
The proposed mechanism requires chemical composition to remain constant between the nanocrystalline and coarse-grained samples.
SLM-produced high-entropy alloys can have improved mechanical properties relative to conventionally processed variants.
Analogous improvements in mechanical and protective properties of high-entropy alloys have been causally linked to grain-boundary density.
The quantitative catalytic contribution of grain boundaries relative to other microstructural features remains unresolved.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant rate increase of at least 20% together with enhanced durability would falsify the hypothesis.
